Daniel’s “laminar flow” analogy is appealing because it gestures at something real: emissions data *can* be propagated through supply chains in a way that avoids naive double-counting, much like cost accounting. But the post smuggles in a crucial assumption—*that a single additive number exists for “the carbon this product is responsible for”* in the same clean way a dollar price exists. Money is a social unit with a single ledger; emissions are physical flows with contested boundaries and nontrivial attribution rules. The minute Daniel says “responsible for,” he has already picked (without naming it) a specific doctrine of allocation: how to apportion shared facilities, joint products (e.g., dairy + beef), recycling credits, land-use change, and capital equipment over time. Those choices are not mere “technical detail”; they are where incentives live, and they are exactly why the field of Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) has spent decades arguing about system boundaries and allocation methods (see [ISO 14040](https://www.iso.org/standard/37456.html)). A label can be *consistent* without being *true* in any singular sense—and the blog would be clearer if it acknowledged that “CEA” is a conventionally-defined accounting quantity (like GDP), not a directly measured property.

A second blind spot is that “local optimization → good global outcome” is precisely what fails for climate unless the CEA number is coupled to an enforcement mechanism that bites. A carbon label may inform consumers, but it does not by itself internalize the externality; it mainly shifts *preferences* among already-available options, and only for the subset of buyers who notice and care. What actually makes local decisions aggregate into lower emissions is a price on carbon (tax/cap) or binding standards—classic Pigouvian logic—after which labels become a helpful complement rather than the engine. Put differently: Daniel’s system makes carbon *legible*; it doesn’t necessarily make carbon *costly*. That distinction matters because firms will rationally optimize for what changes their objective function, not what sits next to the MSRP.

Finally, Daniel is close to reinventing an existing lineage and would strengthen the proposal by naming it: this is essentially product “Scope 3” / value-chain accounting, with a pass-through rule akin to an inventory model. The practical frontier is not blockchain versus centralized bookkeeping; it’s standardization, auditability, and choice of marginal vs average factors (electricity is the canonical example). The most relevant existing blueprint is the [GHG Protocol Product Standard](https://ghgprotocol.org/product-standard), which already defines how to compute and communicate product life-cycle emissions. If Daniel’s goal is a *scalable* “$ + carbon” tag, the high-leverage question is: which boundary/allocations would be mandated (and by whom), and how would disputes be resolved—because the fight over the number is not an implementation detail, it’s the politics of accountability.
